cells.tense: You know when a stretch of practice has done its work, and you let it end there.
cells.ask: Name one thing your practice has finished — say it plainly to someone today, then let the next hour be minutes and no work.
cells.core:
The work gets put down clean. You can tell when hours of the same thing have come to what they were for, and saying so doesn't feel like quitting. You finish, and the finishing is not the end of you. That is rare — most people either stop too early or can't stop at all.

The sign it's working: a run of practice lands, you call it done, and you stay easy about what comes next. The bend now is that closing a thing can feel like a door shutting, so you hold it a little shut yourself. Let one finished thing stand as finished, out loud, and the ease you already have gets to stay in the room.
cells.sheetLine: You can put finished work down and stay open.
cells.verb: bring a stretch of practice through to its finish
cells.place: working alone at the same small light, over and over

cells.tense: You will have this whole practice finished before the last stretch of it is even here.
cells.ask: Pick the one run you're living in now — write down what it still asks of you, not the finished picture — and do only that today.
cells.core:
'Done' is already on the board in your head, and the last stretch hasn't happened yet. The next version, the settled one, is where you're living — so the practicing is really rehearsing the finish, and the finish keeps moving as you practice. A run that isn't over can't be declared over; that's not a lack of will.

The sign it's working: the finish stays in its future, the hour in front of you gets the attention, and you stop announcing ends. The bend is that arriving early feels safer than the slow middle. Let the one unfinished run you're in keep its middle, and the practice does the thing you're trying to do to it.
cells.sheetLine: You keep calling practice done to skip the middle.
cells.verb: bring a stretch of practice through to its finish

cells.tense: You kept the practice open past the point where it had already finished.
cells.ask: Take the smallest piece of your practice and do it all the way through — count it finished and leave it that way for the day.
cells.core:
Nothing gets to be over. There's one more round, one more refinement, one more thing to learn before it counts as finished — so the same run keeps restarting, and the doing doesn't land. What's absent here isn't effort. It's the point where a person lets a thing be complete.

The sign it's working: a small round gets run to its end, and you call it done without adding a lap. The bend is that letting something finish means letting it go, and that felt like too much to risk. Take the smallest piece and run it all the way through rather than around; one finished thing brings the practice back to your hands.
cells.sheetLine: You keep restarting so nothing has to be over.

cells.tense: Your practice is already closing a cycle you keep describing as still open.
cells.ask: Say out loud what you're no longer learning from one practice, and where that leaves you today.
cells.core:
The skill is already built and it holds without you tending it. When a run of work is done, the hands know, and the next thing arrives clean. A practice that has folded into you doesn't need announcing — it shows in how easily you do it, and you step out the way a job finishes itself.

The bend is that you keep filing this one under still-arriving. What you call more study is the same work walking in place. The closer isn't the doer in your story. Say out loud that this stretch is done and see where that leaves you standing.
cells.sheetLine: One practice is finished and you haven't noticed.
